title: Grade 4 HINDU RELIGIOUS EDUCATION — 8.1 Social and National Festivals

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Utsav means festival. This sub-strand studies three celebrations: Maha Shivratri in Hinduism, Paryushan Parva in Jainism, and Madaraka Day as a national day of Kenya. You will learn why each one is kept, which rites belong to it, and how to celebrate in a way that is patriotic, generous and safe.

## Strand 8.0: Utsav (Festivals)
Sub-strand 8.1: Social and National Festivals
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion
b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals
c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## What this sub-strand covers
• Maha Shivratri (Hinduism)
• Paryushan Parva (Jainism)
• Madaraka Day

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we celebrate festivals?
2. How are rites and rituals an important component during celebration of festivals?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: Learner develops social and civic skills when actively participating in the celebration of festivals.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learner develops communication and self-expression skills when writing/typing simple compositions on the festivals.

## Values
• Unity: Learner enhances non-discrimination while doing charity work for inclusive celebrations.
• Patriotism: Learner practises loyalty as they sing the National Anthem and respect the National flag.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Service learning: Learner embraces community service learning while doing charity work for inclusive celebrations.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link to the skills of writing when writing/typing a simple composition on the festivals to the writing skills learnt in English Language.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 8.0 Utsav (Festivals), Sub-strand 8.1 Social and National Festivals

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Why people celebrate festivals

LESSON 1: WHY PEOPLE CELEBRATE FESTIVALS
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a festival is and why communities keep festivals.
• Name the three festivals in this sub-strand.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
A festival gathers people who might otherwise stay apart. Some festivals remember God. Some remember a holy season of forgiveness. Some remember a country and the duty to care for it. All three kinds appear in this sub-strand.

## Notes
### What an utsav does
An utsav, a festival, is a set time for remembering, worshipping, resting from ordinary rush, and meeting other people. Food, music, stories and special clothes often appear. The meaning is larger than the meal. If the meaning is forgotten, the day becomes only noise.

Festivals build social cohesion when everyone is allowed to belong: children and elders, visitors, and people with disabilities. A celebration that shuts people out has missed the point. They also teach. A child who asks 'Why are we doing this?' should receive a true answer, not a shrug.

### The three selected festivals
- **Maha Shivratri** — a Hindu festival of Lord Shiva, kept at night with worship, fasting for those who are able, and a vigil.
- **Paryushan Parva** — a Jain festival of reflection, careful living and forgiveness.
- **Madaraka Day** — a national festival of Kenya, marked on 1 June, remembering self-government and the responsibility that comes with it.

The first two are religious and social. The third is national. All three can teach unity. You do not have to belong to a faith to show respect when neighbours celebrate. You do belong to Kenya, so Madaraka Day is part of your civic life whatever your religion.

### A respectful learner
Learn the correct name of each festival. Do not turn a fast, a prayer or the flag into a joke. Ask before you join a rite that is not from your own home. Joining a school Madaraka Day assembly is for the whole school. Joining puja or a Jain temple rite is by invitation and with a parent or teacher.

Patriotism and faith are not enemies in this lesson. A person can love Kenya and still honour a religious festival with sincerity.

## Key words
• utsav — a festival
• social cohesion — people staying together in respect and belonging
• patriotism — love and loyal service of one's country

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says festivals are only for eating. What else are they for, using the three examples?

Working:
1. Maha Shivratri is for worship of Lord Shiva.
2. Paryushan is for reflection and forgiveness.
3. Madaraka Day is for remembering Kenya's self-government and our responsibility.

Answer: They are also for worship, forgiveness, national memory and coming together.

## Activity: Three festival cards
You will need: Cards, Colour pencils
1. Make one card each for Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
2. On each card write the community that keeps it and one reason it is celebrated.
3. Tell a partner why festivals can build social cohesion.
4. Listen to a short story or account from your teacher about one of the three festivals.

## Practice
1. What does utsav mean?
2. Name the three festivals in this sub-strand.
3. Give one reason communities celebrate festivals.

## Summary
• A festival remembers something important and brings people together.
• The three festivals are Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
• Respect, inclusion and true reasons matter more than noise.

### Answers to practice
1. Festival.
2. Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
3. To remember God or an important event, to worship or forgive, and to bring people together.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: The meaning of Maha Shivratri

LESSON 2: THE MEANING OF MAHA SHIVRATRI
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Explain who Lord Shiva is in this festival and what the night remembers.
• Retell the account of Shiva drinking the poison to save others.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion

## Introduction
Maha Shivratri means the great night of Shiva. Hindu families stay awake, worship, and remember a Lord who is both a yogi on the mountain and a protector of the world. The night is solemn as well as joyful.

## Notes
### Lord Shiva
In Sanatan tradition Lord Shiva is worshipped as the great yogi, the Lord of mercy, and the one who ends evil so that life can continue. He is often shown with a snake, the crescent moon, the river Ganga in his hair, and a trident. A linga in the shrine is a sacred symbol of Shiva, not a toy. Speak of it with respect.

### The great night
Maha Shivratri falls on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight in the month of Phalguna, in the season that matches about February or March. The date on a wall calendar changes from year to year because it follows the traditional calendar. What does not change is the practice: night worship rather than a daytime fair alone.

### The poison and the blue throat
A famous account tells of the churning of the ocean. From the waters came a deadly poison that could have destroyed living beings. Lord Shiva drank it to protect the world. Goddess Parvati held his throat so that the poison would not go further, and his throat turned blue. He is called Neelkanth, the blue-throated one. The story's essence is courage and compassion: he took the harm on himself so that others would live.

### Why the festival builds cohesion
People gather at the mandir who may not meet every week. They sing, wait through the night in turns, and share prasad. Rich and poor can stand in the same queue. That shared wait is social cohesion. The meaning to carry home is not 'stay up to look tired'. It is 'honour Shiva by being brave and kind, and by protecting others from harm'.

## Key words
• Maha Shivratri — the great night of Lord Shiva
• Neelkanth — a name of Shiva meaning the blue-throated one
• linga — the sacred symbol of Lord Shiva worshipped in the shrine

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why is Shiva called Neelkanth in the story told at Maha Shivratri?

Working:
1. He drank the poison that came from the churning of the ocean.
2. It stayed in his throat and turned it blue.
3. The name remembers that act of protection.

Answer: Because the poison he drank to save the world turned his throat blue.

## Activity: Narrate the night of Shiva
You will need: Exercise book
1. Listen to the story of Neelkanth told by your teacher or a resource person.
2. Retell it in order: the poison, Shiva's act, Parvati holding the throat, the world saved.
3. Write one sentence on why this festival can draw a community together.
4. Watch only a video the teacher has approved, and name one true rite you saw, not a scene you invented.

## Practice
1. What does Maha Shivratri mean?
2. What did Lord Shiva do with the poison in the story of the churning of the ocean?
3. Why do people gather at a mandir on this night?

## Summary
• Maha Shivratri is the great night of Lord Shiva.
• The Neelkanth story teaches courage and protection of others.
• The date follows the traditional calendar, in the Phalguna season.

### Answers to practice
1. The great night of Shiva.
2. He drank it to protect the world, and his throat turned blue.
3. To worship Shiva together, keep vigil, sing and share prasad.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Rites of Maha Shivratri

LESSON 3: RITES OF MAHA SHIVRATRI
=================================

## What you will learn
• Identify the main rites of Maha Shivratri.
• Explain how children can take part safely.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals

## Introduction
Knowing the story is one step. Knowing what people actually do on the night is the next. Rites are the actions of the festival: fasting for those who should fast, bathing the linga, offering bel leaves, chanting, and staying awake.

## Notes
### Rites you should be able to name
- **Fasting:** many adults fast or eat only a simple meal. A child fasts only if a parent and the child's health allow it. A harsh fast is not a duty of Grade 4. Drinking water is not a failure.
- **Abhishek:** the linga is bathed with water, and often with milk and other offerings, while prayers are said. This is done by the priest or by worshippers as the mandir directs. Do not pour random liquids.
- **Bel leaves:** leaves of the bel tree are a traditional offering to Shiva. They are offered with respect, not scattered as litter.
- **Chanting:** a common mantra is Om Namah Shivaya, meaning 'I bow to Shiva'. Say it calmly if you have been taught it.
- **Jagarana:** a vigil, staying awake through parts of the night with bhajan and prayer. Children stay with their families and sleep when parents say so.
- **Prasad:** received politely at the end.

### Why rites matter
The rites give everybody the same way to remember the story. Bathing the linga recalls purity and service. The vigil recalls the night itself. The mantra keeps the mind on Shiva rather than on gossip. Without rites, the festival can shrink into noise and fireworks. With rites, the body joins the meaning.

### Safety
Stay with the adult who brought you. Do not play near lamps, oil or a crowded doorway. Do not run down mandir steps. If the night is long, sit when you are tired. Tell a parent if you feel unwell. Include a classmate who wants to watch a school presentation but cannot stand for long: offer a seat near the front.

These rites belong to Hindu worship. Visitors observe them with quiet respect and join only the parts the host invites.

## Key words
• jagarana — a night vigil of prayer and singing
• bel — the tree whose leaves are offered to Lord Shiva
• Om Namah Shivaya — a mantra meaning 'I bow to Shiva'

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A child is told to copy an adult's full fast and to stay awake all night alone at the back of the mandir. What is the safer, still respectful choice?

Working:
1. Children fast only with a parent's decision and if they are well.
2. A vigil is kept with family, not alone in a crowd.
3. The child can still chant, sit for aarti, and receive prasad.

Answer: Stay with the family, join the prayers they choose, drink water if needed, and rest when told.

## Activity: List the rites of the night
You will need: A chart, Pictures chosen by the teacher
1. List the rites: fasting according to ability, abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya, vigil and prasad.
2. Beside each rite write why it is done.
3. Add three safety rules for children.
4. If a video is shown, tick the rites you actually see. Do not tick what was not there.

## Practice
1. Name three rites of Maha Shivratri.
2. What does Om Namah Shivaya mean?
3. Why should a Grade 4 learner not keep a harsh fast just to impress friends?

## Summary
• Rites include worship of the linga, bel leaves, the mantra, vigil and prasad.
• Children follow a parent's guidance on fasting and rest.
• Safety and family company are part of a proper celebration.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: fasting as appropriate, abhishek of the linga, offering bel leaves, chanting Om Namah Shivaya, the night vigil, receiving prasad.
2. I bow to Shiva.
3. Fasting is a religious choice guided by parents and health, not a contest.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: The meaning of Paryushan Parva

LESSON 4: THE MEANING OF PARYUSHAN PARVA
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what Paryushan Parva is and which community celebrates it.
• State the festival's aims of reflection, non-violence and forgiveness.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion

## Introduction
Paryushan Parva is the great holy season of the Jains. It is quieter than many fairs. People look at their own conduct, try to harm no living being, and ask forgiveness from anyone they have hurt.

## Notes
### A season of turning back
Paryushan is a Jain festival of self-review. The name is linked with staying close to the soul and to the teachings. It lasts several days, often eight in Shvetambara communities, and it ends with a day of forgiveness. Digambara Jains keep a related observance called Das Lakshana, lasting ten days, with the same spirit of virtue and forgiveness. You do not need to argue about the number of days. You do need the meaning.

### What people are aiming at
- To remember the Tirthankaras and listen to scripture, including the Kalpasutra in many communities
- To practise ahimsa more carefully, even in small things such as walking attentively and not wasting food
- To speak the truth and to reduce anger
- To forgive and to ask for forgiveness

The forgiveness greeting you should know is **Micchami Dukkadam**. It means: if I have caused you sorrow by thought, word or action, knowingly or unknowingly, may that fault be set aside. People say it to family, friends and even to those they have avoided all year.

### Social cohesion
Asking forgiveness is social, not only private. A class that copies the spirit, even if they are not Jain, might apologise to a classmate they have teased. The festival fails if people fast in public and keep a feud in private. The cohesion comes from repaired relationships.

Appreciate Paryushan by using its real name, by not mocking a person who is eating simply, and by learning the forgiveness greeting accurately.

## Key words
• Paryushan Parva — the Jain festival of reflection, careful conduct and forgiveness
• Micchami Dukkadam — a Jain greeting asking forgiveness for any harm done

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A friend thinks Paryushan is a Hindu night for Lord Shiva. How do you correct the statement kindly?

Working:
1. Maha Shivratri is the Hindu festival of Shiva.
2. Paryushan is a Jain festival.
3. Its special mark is self-review and forgiveness, including the words Micchami Dukkadam.

Answer: Paryushan Parva is Jain. It is a season of reflection and forgiveness, not the night of Shiva.

## Activity: The forgiveness greeting
You will need: The words Micchami Dukkadam written clearly
1. Listen to a short account of Paryushan from your teacher.
2. Practise saying Micchami Dukkadam and write the meaning in your own words.
3. Discuss how a season of forgiveness can hold a community together.
4. Write one true difference between Paryushan and Maha Shivratri.

## Practice
1. Which faith celebrates Paryushan Parva?
2. What does Micchami Dukkadam express?
3. Name two aims of Paryushan.

## Summary
• Paryushan is a Jain festival of reflection, ahimsa and forgiveness.
• Micchami Dukkadam is the greeting that asks pardon.
• It is a different festival from Maha Shivratri.

### Answers to practice
1. Jainism.
2. A request for forgiveness for any harm done by thought, word or action.
3. Any two: self-review, ahimsa, listening to scripture, reducing anger, asking forgiveness.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Rites, charity and inclusion at Paryushan

LESSON 5: RITES, CHARITY AND INCLUSION AT PARYUSHAN
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Identify rites observed during Paryushan.
• Show how charity and inclusion belong to the festival.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
During Paryushan a Jain home may look simpler. Meals change, scripture is heard, and people make time to apologise. Those rites are not empty habits. They train the very forgiveness the festival names.

## Notes
### Rites and practices
- **Pratikraman:** a review of conduct. Worshippers confess faults and resolve to be more careful. Children can understand it as an honest look at the day.
- **Scripture:** many families listen to the life of Mahavira and other readings. Silence during the reading is part of the rite.
- **Fasting and simple food:** adults may fast. Children follow what their own parents decide. Guests do not tease a person who refuses a feast.
- **Care for living beings:** people avoid harm, waste and harsh speech more strictly than usual.
- **Samvatsari or the forgiveness day:** the season closes with Micchami Dukkadam said face to face or by message. In communities that use another closing day within Das Lakshana, forgiveness is still the heart.
- **Visiting the derasar:** shoes off, clean clothes, quiet voice.

### Charity and inclusion
The design asks for charity that makes celebrations inclusive. During a holy season that can mean sharing food with someone who has less, visiting a person who cannot reach the temple, or making sure a classmate with a disability can hear the story. Charity is not a show of money. A shared pencil, a carried chair, or a sincere apology can be the honest gift.

Service learning means the help is real. If the class collects items, they should reach the people who were named, and the list of what was given should be true.

### Appreciation
You appreciate Paryushan when you let its rites teach you even as a guest: sit still, do not waste food that day, and say sorry where you owe an apology. You do not need to pretend you are Jain in order to respect a Jain festival.

## Key words
• pratikraman — a Jain review of one's conduct, with confession and a fresh resolve
• derasar — a Jain temple

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class wants to include a classmate who uses a wheelchair in a Paryushan story afternoon. What preparations show real inclusion?

Working:
1. Choose a room the classmate can enter.
2. Reserve a space that does not block the doorway.
3. Explain the meaning of Micchami Dukkadam so they can take part in the discussion, not only sit at the side.

Answer: Make the room accessible, keep a proper space, and include them in the learning.

## Activity: Inclusive kindness
You will need: Paper, A small class charity plan approved by the teacher
1. List the rites of Paryushan in your book.
2. Plan one inclusive act: an apology card, a shared reading with a seat for every learner, or a small gift of food organised with the teacher.
3. Do the act. Do not leave anyone out because the work is slow.
4. Write how the act fits the festival's spirit of forgiveness and non-violence.

## Practice
1. What is pratikraman?
2. Name one rite at the end of Paryushan.
3. Give one inclusive act that fits the festival.

## Summary
• Paryushan rites include self-review, scripture, careful food, ahimsa and a day of forgiveness.
• Charity should include people who are often left out.
• Guests respect the rites even when they are not Jain.

### Answers to practice
1. A review of one's conduct, admitting faults and resolving to do better.
2. Asking forgiveness, often with the words Micchami Dukkadam.
3. Any one: sharing food, making room for a classmate with a disability, or apologising to someone you hurt.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Madaraka Day

LESSON 6: MADARAKA DAY
======================

## What you will learn
• State when Madaraka Day is marked and what it remembers.
• Explain how the day can build patriotism and unity.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
Not every festival belongs to one religion. Madaraka Day belongs to Kenya. It is marked on 1 June. The day remembers when Kenya received internal self-government, and it asks citizens to carry responsibility, not only to cheer.

## Notes
### The date and the meaning
Madaraka Day is 1 June. In 1963 Kenya attained internal self-government, called Madaraka. The Kiswahili word madaraka means power or responsibility to govern. Full independence, remembered on Jamhuri Day, came later, on 12 December 1963. Do not swap the two days. Madaraka is 1 June. Jamhuri is 12 December.

The festival is national. People of every faith can stand together for it. That is social cohesion of a civic kind: Hindu, Jain, Sikh, Buddhist, Christian, Muslim and other Kenyan children in one assembly.

### How it is celebrated
Schools and public gatherings raise the national flag, sing the National Anthem, and listen to speeches about service. There may be parades, poems, music and dance. A community may visit a hall, a stadium or a museum when such a visit is organised safely. Photos should be taken only with permission.

### Patriotism that is practical
Patriotism is loyalty to the country. On this day it looks like:
- Standing still and singing the anthem with respect
- Learning what the flag means and not dragging it on the ground
- Talking about responsibility: caring for school property, obeying just laws, and refusing tribal insults
- Including every learner in the performance or the audience

Cheering is easy. Madaraka, responsibility, is the harder gift. A Kenyan who loves the flag but cheats and litters has not yet taken the meaning home. The day asks you to be a citizen who can be trusted with the country's future.

## Key words
• Madaraka Day — Kenya's national day on 1 June, remembering internal self-government and responsibility
• madaraka — power or responsibility to govern
• self-government — a people governing their own affairs

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A quiz asks which date is Madaraka Day and which is Jamhuri Day. Give both without mixing them.

Working:
1. Madaraka Day is 1 June. It marks internal self-government in 1963.
2. Jamhuri Day is 12 December. It marks independence.
3. The word madaraka points to responsibility.

Answer: Madaraka Day is 1 June. Jamhuri Day is 12 December.

## Activity: A short composition on Madaraka
You will need: Exercise book
1. Listen to an account of why 1 June is marked.
2. Write a short composition: what Madaraka means, and one responsibility a learner can carry at school.
3. Read two compositions aloud. Clap for clear, true sentences.
4. Include a classmate who wants to dictate their composition while you write it fairly in their words.

## Practice
1. On which date is Madaraka Day?
2. What did Kenya attain in 1963 that this day remembers?
3. How is Madaraka Day different from a religious festival such as Paryushan?

## Summary
• Madaraka Day is 1 June and remembers Kenya's internal self-government in 1963.
• The name means responsibility.
• Patriotism includes respect for the anthem and fair treatment of every Kenyan.

### Answers to practice
1. 1 June.
2. Internal self-government, called Madaraka.
3. It is a national day for all Kenyans, not a rite of one faith.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: The flag, the anthem and loyalty

LESSON 7: THE FLAG, THE ANTHEM AND LOYALTY
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe respectful behaviour during the National Anthem and flag ceremony.
• Explain the colours and emblem of the Kenyan flag in simple, true words.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
On Madaraka Day the flag and the anthem are not decorations. They are signs of a whole country. The way you stand, sing and handle those signs shows whether patriotism is real.

## Notes
### The National Anthem
Kenya's anthem begins with the words Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu. When it is sung or played:
- Stand still if you are able. A learner who uses a wheelchair remains still and attentive in the chair.
- Face the flag if it is being raised.
- Do not talk, laugh, chew or walk about.
- Sing the words you know correctly. Do not invent silly versions.
- Remove a cap if that is the school custom, unless your faith requires a head covering, which you may keep.

The anthem is a prayer for the nation's unity and strength. Mocking it is a refusal of the festival's meaning.

### The flag
The Kenyan flag has black, red and green bands separated by thin white lines, and a shield with two spears. In the usual teaching of the flag:
- Black stands for the people of Kenya.
- Red stands for the blood shed in the struggle for freedom.
- Green stands for the country's natural wealth and land.
- White stands for peace.
- The shield and spears stand for defence of that freedom and peace.

Do not let the flag touch the ground. Do not sit on it or use it as a costume for a joke. If you help to raise it, follow the teacher's instructions exactly. If it is raining on an outdoor ceremony, adults will decide how the flag is protected.

### Loyalty after the ceremony
Loyalty continues when the assembly ends. It looks like refusing ethnic insults, looking after public property, and telling the truth about your own country: proud of what is good, honest about the duty still to be done. Patriotism is not hatred of neighbours. Kenya's peace depends on citizens who respect one another.

## Key words
• National Anthem — the official song of the country, sung with respect
• emblem — the shield and spears on the Kenyan flag

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During the anthem a learner chats and then drapes a flag over their shoulders for a funny photo. What should they do instead?

Working:
1. Stand still and keep silent or sing.
2. The flag is not a costume for a joke.
3. They should apologise and follow the ceremony properly next time.

Answer: Stand respectfully, do not joke with the flag, and treat both anthem and flag as national signs.

## Activity: Practise the ceremony
You will need: The school flag if the teacher provides it, Space to stand
1. Practise standing still while the teacher leads the opening of the anthem. Do not change the words.
2. Name the colours black, red, green and white and say what each stands for.
3. Practise a respectful flag moment: no dragging, no sitting on the cloth, hands only where the teacher shows.
4. Discuss one way loyalty can appear on an ordinary school day after Madaraka Day is over.

## Practice
1. How should you behave when the National Anthem is sung?
2. What do the black, red, green and white of the Kenyan flag stand for?
3. Why should the flag not be used as a joke costume?

## Summary
• Stand still and sing the anthem with respect.
• The flag's black, red, green and white, with shield and spears, are national signs.
• Loyalty continues in fair speech and care of public things.

### Answers to practice
1. Stand still if you are able, face the flag, and sing or keep silent without talking or laughing.
2. Black for the people, red for the blood shed for freedom, green for the land, and white for peace.
3. It is a national emblem and should be handled with loyalty and respect.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: Celebrating together safely

LESSON 8: CELEBRATING TOGETHER SAFELY
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Compare the rites of the three festivals without mixing them up.
• List safety and inclusion rules for any celebration.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
A good festival can still become dangerous if a crowd pushes, if fire is treated as a toy, or if some children are left outside the gate. This lesson gathers the rites you know and adds the care that lets everyone go home safely.

## Notes
### Keep the rites distinct
- **Maha Shivratri:** night worship of Shiva, abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya, vigil, prasad.
- **Paryushan:** self-review, scripture, ahimsa, simple food or fasting as the family directs, Micchami Dukkadam.
- **Madaraka Day:** flag, National Anthem, speeches, songs and dances of the nation, talk of responsibility.

Mixing them shows you have not really learned them. Bel leaves are not a Madaraka rite. The national flag is not a Jain altar. Respect each pattern.

### Safety for every celebration
- Go and return with a known adult.
- Agree a meeting place if a crowd is large.
- Do not push on stairs, near roads, or towards a stage.
- Do not play with lamps, matches, oil or fireworks.
- Drink safe water. Do not accept food or a lift from a stranger.
- Tell the adult if you feel lost or ill.
- Sensitise a friend who may not hear instructions well: face them, speak clearly, and show the exit.

### Inclusion and charity
Save a seat. Teach a dance step slowly. Share food without insulting someone's diet. A fast should not become a reason to mock. A national dance should not become a reason to leave a shy learner in the corridor. Charity includes people of every faith and none.

Write a short composition that names one festival, two rites, and two safety rules. That piece of writing is your evidence that celebration and care belong together.

## Key words
• vigil — staying awake to pray and watch through a holy time
• inclusion — making sure people are not left out of an activity

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these actions under the right festival: Micchami Dukkadam, raising the flag, offering bel leaves.

Working:
1. Micchami Dukkadam belongs to Paryushan.
2. Raising the Kenyan flag belongs to Madaraka Day.
3. Bel leaves are offered at Maha Shivratri.

Answer: Paryushan; Madaraka Day; Maha Shivratri.

## Activity: Safety talk and a composition
You will need: Exercise book
1. In groups, list safety rules for a night vigil, a crowded temple or hall, and a national ceremony.
2. Add one inclusion rule and one charity idea.
3. Teach the rules to a partner, especially a partner who needs them repeated slowly and clearly.
4. Write a short composition on one festival, its meaning, two rites and how you will stay safe.

## Practice
1. Match bel leaves, Micchami Dukkadam and the National Anthem to their festivals.
2. Name two safety rules for a festival crowd.
3. Why should a celebration include learners with special needs?

## Summary
• Each festival keeps its own rites.
• Crowds, fire and strangers need clear safety rules.
• Inclusion and charity make the celebration fit the values of unity and patriotism.

### Answers to practice
1. Bel leaves: Maha Shivratri. Micchami Dukkadam: Paryushan. National Anthem: Madaraka Day.
2. Any two: stay with a known adult, do not push, do not play with fire, do not go with a stranger, agree a meeting place.
3. Festivals are for social cohesion and unity. Leaving people out contradicts that meaning.

ANSWERS — 8.1 SOCIAL AND NATIONAL FESTIVALS
========================================

1. A. Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day
   The design selects these three: one Hindu, one Jain and one national.

2. B. The great night of Lord Shiva
   It is the Hindu festival of Lord Shiva's great night.

3. B. Because the poison he drank to protect the world turned his throat blue
   The churning-of-the-ocean account explains the blue throat.

4. A. Abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya and a vigil
   Those are acts of Shiva worship on that night.

   Jains observe Paryushan with self-review, ahimsa and forgiveness.

   It is the Jain forgiveness greeting.

   Respect for the anthem is part of patriotism on a national day.

   White stands for peace. Black, red and green stand for the people, the blood shed for freedom, and the land.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Utsav means festival. This sub-strand studies three celebrations: Maha Shivratri in Hinduism, Paryushan Parva in Jainism, and Madaraka Day as a national day of Kenya. You will learn why each one is kept, which rites belong to it, and how to celebrate in a way that is patriotic, generous and safe.

## Strand 8.0: Utsav (Festivals)
Sub-strand 8.1: Social and National Festivals
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion
b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals
c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## What this sub-strand covers
• Maha Shivratri (Hinduism)
• Paryushan Parva (Jainism)
• Madaraka Day

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we celebrate festivals?
2. How are rites and rituals an important component during celebration of festivals?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: Learner develops social and civic skills when actively participating in the celebration of festivals.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learner develops communication and self-expression skills when writing/typing simple compositions on the festivals.

## Values
• Unity: Learner enhances non-discrimination while doing charity work for inclusive celebrations.
• Patriotism: Learner practises loyalty as they sing the National Anthem and respect the National flag.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Service learning: Learner embraces community service learning while doing charity work for inclusive celebrations.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link to the skills of writing when writing/typing a simple composition on the festivals to the writing skills learnt in English Language.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 8.0 Utsav (Festivals), Sub-strand 8.1 Social and National Festivals

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Why people celebrate festivals
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHY PEOPLE CELEBRATE FESTIVALS
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a festival is and why communities keep festivals.
• Name the three festivals in this sub-strand.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
A festival gathers people who might otherwise stay apart. Some festivals remember God. Some remember a holy season of forgiveness. Some remember a country and the duty to care for it. All three kinds appear in this sub-strand.

## Notes
### What an utsav does
An utsav, a festival, is a set time for remembering, worshipping, resting from ordinary rush, and meeting other people. Food, music, stories and special clothes often appear. The meaning is larger than the meal. If the meaning is forgotten, the day becomes only noise.

Festivals build social cohesion when everyone is allowed to belong: children and elders, visitors, and people with disabilities. A celebration that shuts people out has missed the point. They also teach. A child who asks 'Why are we doing this?' should receive a true answer, not a shrug.

### The three selected festivals
- **Maha Shivratri** — a Hindu festival of Lord Shiva, kept at night with worship, fasting for those who are able, and a vigil.
- **Paryushan Parva** — a Jain festival of reflection, careful living and forgiveness.
- **Madaraka Day** — a national festival of Kenya, marked on 1 June, remembering self-government and the responsibility that comes with it.

The first two are religious and social. The third is national. All three can teach unity. You do not have to belong to a faith to show respect when neighbours celebrate. You do belong to Kenya, so Madaraka Day is part of your civic life whatever your religion.

### A respectful learner
Learn the correct name of each festival. Do not turn a fast, a prayer or the flag into a joke. Ask before you join a rite that is not from your own home. Joining a school Madaraka Day assembly is for the whole school. Joining puja or a Jain temple rite is by invitation and with a parent or teacher.

Patriotism and faith are not enemies in this lesson. A person can love Kenya and still honour a religious festival with sincerity.

## Key words
• utsav — a festival
• social cohesion — people staying together in respect and belonging
• patriotism — love and loyal service of one's country

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says festivals are only for eating. What else are they for, using the three examples?

Working:
1. Maha Shivratri is for worship of Lord Shiva.
2. Paryushan is for reflection and forgiveness.
3. Madaraka Day is for remembering Kenya's self-government and our responsibility.

Answer: They are also for worship, forgiveness, national memory and coming together.

## Activity: Three festival cards
You will need: Cards, Colour pencils
1. Make one card each for Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
2. On each card write the community that keeps it and one reason it is celebrated.
3. Tell a partner why festivals can build social cohesion.
4. Listen to a short story or account from your teacher about one of the three festivals.

## Practice
1. What does utsav mean?
2. Name the three festivals in this sub-strand.
3. Give one reason communities celebrate festivals.

## Summary
• A festival remembers something important and brings people together.
• The three festivals are Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
• Respect, inclusion and true reasons matter more than noise.

### Answers to practice
1. Festival.
2. Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day.
3. To remember God or an important event, to worship or forgive, and to bring people together.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The meaning of Maha Shivratri
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: THE MEANING OF MAHA SHIVRATRI
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Explain who Lord Shiva is in this festival and what the night remembers.
• Retell the account of Shiva drinking the poison to save others.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion

## Introduction
Maha Shivratri means the great night of Shiva. Hindu families stay awake, worship, and remember a Lord who is both a yogi on the mountain and a protector of the world. The night is solemn as well as joyful.

## Notes
### Lord Shiva
In Sanatan tradition Lord Shiva is worshipped as the great yogi, the Lord of mercy, and the one who ends evil so that life can continue. He is often shown with a snake, the crescent moon, the river Ganga in his hair, and a trident. A linga in the shrine is a sacred symbol of Shiva, not a toy. Speak of it with respect.

### The great night
Maha Shivratri falls on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight in the month of Phalguna, in the season that matches about February or March. The date on a wall calendar changes from year to year because it follows the traditional calendar. What does not change is the practice: night worship rather than a daytime fair alone.

### The poison and the blue throat
A famous account tells of the churning of the ocean. From the waters came a deadly poison that could have destroyed living beings. Lord Shiva drank it to protect the world. Goddess Parvati held his throat so that the poison would not go further, and his throat turned blue. He is called Neelkanth, the blue-throated one. The story's essence is courage and compassion: he took the harm on himself so that others would live.

### Why the festival builds cohesion
People gather at the mandir who may not meet every week. They sing, wait through the night in turns, and share prasad. Rich and poor can stand in the same queue. That shared wait is social cohesion. The meaning to carry home is not 'stay up to look tired'. It is 'honour Shiva by being brave and kind, and by protecting others from harm'.

## Key words
• Maha Shivratri — the great night of Lord Shiva
• Neelkanth — a name of Shiva meaning the blue-throated one
• linga — the sacred symbol of Lord Shiva worshipped in the shrine

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why is Shiva called Neelkanth in the story told at Maha Shivratri?

Working:
1. He drank the poison that came from the churning of the ocean.
2. It stayed in his throat and turned it blue.
3. The name remembers that act of protection.

Answer: Because the poison he drank to save the world turned his throat blue.

## Activity: Narrate the night of Shiva
You will need: Exercise book
1. Listen to the story of Neelkanth told by your teacher or a resource person.
2. Retell it in order: the poison, Shiva's act, Parvati holding the throat, the world saved.
3. Write one sentence on why this festival can draw a community together.
4. Watch only a video the teacher has approved, and name one true rite you saw, not a scene you invented.

## Practice
1. What does Maha Shivratri mean?
2. What did Lord Shiva do with the poison in the story of the churning of the ocean?
3. Why do people gather at a mandir on this night?

## Summary
• Maha Shivratri is the great night of Lord Shiva.
• The Neelkanth story teaches courage and protection of others.
• The date follows the traditional calendar, in the Phalguna season.

### Answers to practice
1. The great night of Shiva.
2. He drank it to protect the world, and his throat turned blue.
3. To worship Shiva together, keep vigil, sing and share prasad.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Rites of Maha Shivratri
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: RITES OF MAHA SHIVRATRI
=================================

## What you will learn
• Identify the main rites of Maha Shivratri.
• Explain how children can take part safely.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals

## Introduction
Knowing the story is one step. Knowing what people actually do on the night is the next. Rites are the actions of the festival: fasting for those who should fast, bathing the linga, offering bel leaves, chanting, and staying awake.

## Notes
### Rites you should be able to name
- **Fasting:** many adults fast or eat only a simple meal. A child fasts only if a parent and the child's health allow it. A harsh fast is not a duty of Grade 4. Drinking water is not a failure.
- **Abhishek:** the linga is bathed with water, and often with milk and other offerings, while prayers are said. This is done by the priest or by worshippers as the mandir directs. Do not pour random liquids.
- **Bel leaves:** leaves of the bel tree are a traditional offering to Shiva. They are offered with respect, not scattered as litter.
- **Chanting:** a common mantra is Om Namah Shivaya, meaning 'I bow to Shiva'. Say it calmly if you have been taught it.
- **Jagarana:** a vigil, staying awake through parts of the night with bhajan and prayer. Children stay with their families and sleep when parents say so.
- **Prasad:** received politely at the end.

### Why rites matter
The rites give everybody the same way to remember the story. Bathing the linga recalls purity and service. The vigil recalls the night itself. The mantra keeps the mind on Shiva rather than on gossip. Without rites, the festival can shrink into noise and fireworks. With rites, the body joins the meaning.

### Safety
Stay with the adult who brought you. Do not play near lamps, oil or a crowded doorway. Do not run down mandir steps. If the night is long, sit when you are tired. Tell a parent if you feel unwell. Include a classmate who wants to watch a school presentation but cannot stand for long: offer a seat near the front.

These rites belong to Hindu worship. Visitors observe them with quiet respect and join only the parts the host invites.

## Key words
• jagarana — a night vigil of prayer and singing
• bel — the tree whose leaves are offered to Lord Shiva
• Om Namah Shivaya — a mantra meaning 'I bow to Shiva'

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A child is told to copy an adult's full fast and to stay awake all night alone at the back of the mandir. What is the safer, still respectful choice?

Working:
1. Children fast only with a parent's decision and if they are well.
2. A vigil is kept with family, not alone in a crowd.
3. The child can still chant, sit for aarti, and receive prasad.

Answer: Stay with the family, join the prayers they choose, drink water if needed, and rest when told.

## Activity: List the rites of the night
You will need: A chart, Pictures chosen by the teacher
1. List the rites: fasting according to ability, abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya, vigil and prasad.
2. Beside each rite write why it is done.
3. Add three safety rules for children.
4. If a video is shown, tick the rites you actually see. Do not tick what was not there.

## Practice
1. Name three rites of Maha Shivratri.
2. What does Om Namah Shivaya mean?
3. Why should a Grade 4 learner not keep a harsh fast just to impress friends?

## Summary
• Rites include worship of the linga, bel leaves, the mantra, vigil and prasad.
• Children follow a parent's guidance on fasting and rest.
• Safety and family company are part of a proper celebration.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: fasting as appropriate, abhishek of the linga, offering bel leaves, chanting Om Namah Shivaya, the night vigil, receiving prasad.
2. I bow to Shiva.
3. Fasting is a religious choice guided by parents and health, not a contest.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: The meaning of Paryushan Parva
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: THE MEANING OF PARYUSHAN PARVA
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what Paryushan Parva is and which community celebrates it.
• State the festival's aims of reflection, non-violence and forgiveness.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion

## Introduction
Paryushan Parva is the great holy season of the Jains. It is quieter than many fairs. People look at their own conduct, try to harm no living being, and ask forgiveness from anyone they have hurt.

## Notes
### A season of turning back
Paryushan is a Jain festival of self-review. The name is linked with staying close to the soul and to the teachings. It lasts several days, often eight in Shvetambara communities, and it ends with a day of forgiveness. Digambara Jains keep a related observance called Das Lakshana, lasting ten days, with the same spirit of virtue and forgiveness. You do not need to argue about the number of days. You do need the meaning.

### What people are aiming at
- To remember the Tirthankaras and listen to scripture, including the Kalpasutra in many communities
- To practise ahimsa more carefully, even in small things such as walking attentively and not wasting food
- To speak the truth and to reduce anger
- To forgive and to ask for forgiveness

The forgiveness greeting you should know is **Micchami Dukkadam**. It means: if I have caused you sorrow by thought, word or action, knowingly or unknowingly, may that fault be set aside. People say it to family, friends and even to those they have avoided all year.

### Social cohesion
Asking forgiveness is social, not only private. A class that copies the spirit, even if they are not Jain, might apologise to a classmate they have teased. The festival fails if people fast in public and keep a feud in private. The cohesion comes from repaired relationships.

Appreciate Paryushan by using its real name, by not mocking a person who is eating simply, and by learning the forgiveness greeting accurately.

## Key words
• Paryushan Parva — the Jain festival of reflection, careful conduct and forgiveness
• Micchami Dukkadam — a Jain greeting asking forgiveness for any harm done

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A friend thinks Paryushan is a Hindu night for Lord Shiva. How do you correct the statement kindly?

Working:
1. Maha Shivratri is the Hindu festival of Shiva.
2. Paryushan is a Jain festival.
3. Its special mark is self-review and forgiveness, including the words Micchami Dukkadam.

Answer: Paryushan Parva is Jain. It is a season of reflection and forgiveness, not the night of Shiva.

## Activity: The forgiveness greeting
You will need: The words Micchami Dukkadam written clearly
1. Listen to a short account of Paryushan from your teacher.
2. Practise saying Micchami Dukkadam and write the meaning in your own words.
3. Discuss how a season of forgiveness can hold a community together.
4. Write one true difference between Paryushan and Maha Shivratri.

## Practice
1. Which faith celebrates Paryushan Parva?
2. What does Micchami Dukkadam express?
3. Name two aims of Paryushan.

## Summary
• Paryushan is a Jain festival of reflection, ahimsa and forgiveness.
• Micchami Dukkadam is the greeting that asks pardon.
• It is a different festival from Maha Shivratri.

### Answers to practice
1. Jainism.
2. A request for forgiveness for any harm done by thought, word or action.
3. Any two: self-review, ahimsa, listening to scripture, reducing anger, asking forgiveness.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Rites, charity and inclusion at Paryushan
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: RITES, CHARITY AND INCLUSION AT PARYUSHAN
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Identify rites observed during Paryushan.
• Show how charity and inclusion belong to the festival.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
During Paryushan a Jain home may look simpler. Meals change, scripture is heard, and people make time to apologise. Those rites are not empty habits. They train the very forgiveness the festival names.

## Notes
### Rites and practices
- **Pratikraman:** a review of conduct. Worshippers confess faults and resolve to be more careful. Children can understand it as an honest look at the day.
- **Scripture:** many families listen to the life of Mahavira and other readings. Silence during the reading is part of the rite.
- **Fasting and simple food:** adults may fast. Children follow what their own parents decide. Guests do not tease a person who refuses a feast.
- **Care for living beings:** people avoid harm, waste and harsh speech more strictly than usual.
- **Samvatsari or the forgiveness day:** the season closes with Micchami Dukkadam said face to face or by message. In communities that use another closing day within Das Lakshana, forgiveness is still the heart.
- **Visiting the derasar:** shoes off, clean clothes, quiet voice.

### Charity and inclusion
The design asks for charity that makes celebrations inclusive. During a holy season that can mean sharing food with someone who has less, visiting a person who cannot reach the temple, or making sure a classmate with a disability can hear the story. Charity is not a show of money. A shared pencil, a carried chair, or a sincere apology can be the honest gift.

Service learning means the help is real. If the class collects items, they should reach the people who were named, and the list of what was given should be true.

### Appreciation
You appreciate Paryushan when you let its rites teach you even as a guest: sit still, do not waste food that day, and say sorry where you owe an apology. You do not need to pretend you are Jain in order to respect a Jain festival.

## Key words
• pratikraman — a Jain review of one's conduct, with confession and a fresh resolve
• derasar — a Jain temple

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class wants to include a classmate who uses a wheelchair in a Paryushan story afternoon. What preparations show real inclusion?

Working:
1. Choose a room the classmate can enter.
2. Reserve a space that does not block the doorway.
3. Explain the meaning of Micchami Dukkadam so they can take part in the discussion, not only sit at the side.

Answer: Make the room accessible, keep a proper space, and include them in the learning.

## Activity: Inclusive kindness
You will need: Paper, A small class charity plan approved by the teacher
1. List the rites of Paryushan in your book.
2. Plan one inclusive act: an apology card, a shared reading with a seat for every learner, or a small gift of food organised with the teacher.
3. Do the act. Do not leave anyone out because the work is slow.
4. Write how the act fits the festival's spirit of forgiveness and non-violence.

## Practice
1. What is pratikraman?
2. Name one rite at the end of Paryushan.
3. Give one inclusive act that fits the festival.

## Summary
• Paryushan rites include self-review, scripture, careful food, ahimsa and a day of forgiveness.
• Charity should include people who are often left out.
• Guests respect the rites even when they are not Jain.

### Answers to practice
1. A review of one's conduct, admitting faults and resolving to do better.
2. Asking forgiveness, often with the words Micchami Dukkadam.
3. Any one: sharing food, making room for a classmate with a disability, or apologising to someone you hurt.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Madaraka Day
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: MADARAKA DAY
======================

## What you will learn
• State when Madaraka Day is marked and what it remembers.
• Explain how the day can build patriotism and unity.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the significance of celebrating the three selected festivals for social cohesion; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
Not every festival belongs to one religion. Madaraka Day belongs to Kenya. It is marked on 1 June. The day remembers when Kenya received internal self-government, and it asks citizens to carry responsibility, not only to cheer.

## Notes
### The date and the meaning
Madaraka Day is 1 June. In 1963 Kenya attained internal self-government, called Madaraka. The Kiswahili word madaraka means power or responsibility to govern. Full independence, remembered on Jamhuri Day, came later, on 12 December 1963. Do not swap the two days. Madaraka is 1 June. Jamhuri is 12 December.

The festival is national. People of every faith can stand together for it. That is social cohesion of a civic kind: Hindu, Jain, Sikh, Buddhist, Christian, Muslim and other Kenyan children in one assembly.

### How it is celebrated
Schools and public gatherings raise the national flag, sing the National Anthem, and listen to speeches about service. There may be parades, poems, music and dance. A community may visit a hall, a stadium or a museum when such a visit is organised safely. Photos should be taken only with permission.

### Patriotism that is practical
Patriotism is loyalty to the country. On this day it looks like:
- Standing still and singing the anthem with respect
- Learning what the flag means and not dragging it on the ground
- Talking about responsibility: caring for school property, obeying just laws, and refusing tribal insults
- Including every learner in the performance or the audience

Cheering is easy. Madaraka, responsibility, is the harder gift. A Kenyan who loves the flag but cheats and litters has not yet taken the meaning home. The day asks you to be a citizen who can be trusted with the country's future.

## Key words
• Madaraka Day — Kenya's national day on 1 June, remembering internal self-government and responsibility
• madaraka — power or responsibility to govern
• self-government — a people governing their own affairs

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A quiz asks which date is Madaraka Day and which is Jamhuri Day. Give both without mixing them.

Working:
1. Madaraka Day is 1 June. It marks internal self-government in 1963.
2. Jamhuri Day is 12 December. It marks independence.
3. The word madaraka points to responsibility.

Answer: Madaraka Day is 1 June. Jamhuri Day is 12 December.

## Activity: A short composition on Madaraka
You will need: Exercise book
1. Listen to an account of why 1 June is marked.
2. Write a short composition: what Madaraka means, and one responsibility a learner can carry at school.
3. Read two compositions aloud. Clap for clear, true sentences.
4. Include a classmate who wants to dictate their composition while you write it fairly in their words.

## Practice
1. On which date is Madaraka Day?
2. What did Kenya attain in 1963 that this day remembers?
3. How is Madaraka Day different from a religious festival such as Paryushan?

## Summary
• Madaraka Day is 1 June and remembers Kenya's internal self-government in 1963.
• The name means responsibility.
• Patriotism includes respect for the anthem and fair treatment of every Kenyan.

### Answers to practice
1. 1 June.
2. Internal self-government, called Madaraka.
3. It is a national day for all Kenyans, not a rite of one faith.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: The flag, the anthem and loyalty
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: THE FLAG, THE ANTHEM AND LOYALTY
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe respectful behaviour during the National Anthem and flag ceremony.
• Explain the colours and emblem of the Kenyan flag in simple, true words.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
On Madaraka Day the flag and the anthem are not decorations. They are signs of a whole country. The way you stand, sing and handle those signs shows whether patriotism is real.

## Notes
### The National Anthem
Kenya's anthem begins with the words Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu. When it is sung or played:
- Stand still if you are able. A learner who uses a wheelchair remains still and attentive in the chair.
- Face the flag if it is being raised.
- Do not talk, laugh, chew or walk about.
- Sing the words you know correctly. Do not invent silly versions.
- Remove a cap if that is the school custom, unless your faith requires a head covering, which you may keep.

The anthem is a prayer for the nation's unity and strength. Mocking it is a refusal of the festival's meaning.

### The flag
The Kenyan flag has black, red and green bands separated by thin white lines, and a shield with two spears. In the usual teaching of the flag:
- Black stands for the people of Kenya.
- Red stands for the blood shed in the struggle for freedom.
- Green stands for the country's natural wealth and land.
- White stands for peace.
- The shield and spears stand for defence of that freedom and peace.

Do not let the flag touch the ground. Do not sit on it or use it as a costume for a joke. If you help to raise it, follow the teacher's instructions exactly. If it is raining on an outdoor ceremony, adults will decide how the flag is protected.

### Loyalty after the ceremony
Loyalty continues when the assembly ends. It looks like refusing ethnic insults, looking after public property, and telling the truth about your own country: proud of what is good, honest about the duty still to be done. Patriotism is not hatred of neighbours. Kenya's peace depends on citizens who respect one another.

## Key words
• National Anthem — the official song of the country, sung with respect
• emblem — the shield and spears on the Kenyan flag

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During the anthem a learner chats and then drapes a flag over their shoulders for a funny photo. What should they do instead?

Working:
1. Stand still and keep silent or sing.
2. The flag is not a costume for a joke.
3. They should apologise and follow the ceremony properly next time.

Answer: Stand respectfully, do not joke with the flag, and treat both anthem and flag as national signs.

## Activity: Practise the ceremony
You will need: The school flag if the teacher provides it, Space to stand
1. Practise standing still while the teacher leads the opening of the anthem. Do not change the words.
2. Name the colours black, red, green and white and say what each stands for.
3. Practise a respectful flag moment: no dragging, no sitting on the cloth, hands only where the teacher shows.
4. Discuss one way loyalty can appear on an ordinary school day after Madaraka Day is over.

## Practice
1. How should you behave when the National Anthem is sung?
2. What do the black, red, green and white of the Kenyan flag stand for?
3. Why should the flag not be used as a joke costume?

## Summary
• Stand still and sing the anthem with respect.
• The flag's black, red, green and white, with shield and spears, are national signs.
• Loyalty continues in fair speech and care of public things.

### Answers to practice
1. Stand still if you are able, face the flag, and sing or keep silent without talking or laughing.
2. Black for the people, red for the blood shed for freedom, green for the land, and white for peace.
3. It is a national emblem and should be handled with loyalty and respect.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Celebrating together safely
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: CELEBRATING TOGETHER SAFELY
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Compare the rites of the three festivals without mixing them up.
• List safety and inclusion rules for any celebration.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify the rites and rituals during the celebration of different festivals; c) appreciate the significance of celebrating social and national festivals for patriotism

## Introduction
A good festival can still become dangerous if a crowd pushes, if fire is treated as a toy, or if some children are left outside the gate. This lesson gathers the rites you know and adds the care that lets everyone go home safely.

## Notes
### Keep the rites distinct
- **Maha Shivratri:** night worship of Shiva, abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya, vigil, prasad.
- **Paryushan:** self-review, scripture, ahimsa, simple food or fasting as the family directs, Micchami Dukkadam.
- **Madaraka Day:** flag, National Anthem, speeches, songs and dances of the nation, talk of responsibility.

Mixing them shows you have not really learned them. Bel leaves are not a Madaraka rite. The national flag is not a Jain altar. Respect each pattern.

### Safety for every celebration
- Go and return with a known adult.
- Agree a meeting place if a crowd is large.
- Do not push on stairs, near roads, or towards a stage.
- Do not play with lamps, matches, oil or fireworks.
- Drink safe water. Do not accept food or a lift from a stranger.
- Tell the adult if you feel lost or ill.
- Sensitise a friend who may not hear instructions well: face them, speak clearly, and show the exit.

### Inclusion and charity
Save a seat. Teach a dance step slowly. Share food without insulting someone's diet. A fast should not become a reason to mock. A national dance should not become a reason to leave a shy learner in the corridor. Charity includes people of every faith and none.

Write a short composition that names one festival, two rites, and two safety rules. That piece of writing is your evidence that celebration and care belong together.

## Key words
• vigil — staying awake to pray and watch through a holy time
• inclusion — making sure people are not left out of an activity

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these actions under the right festival: Micchami Dukkadam, raising the flag, offering bel leaves.

Working:
1. Micchami Dukkadam belongs to Paryushan.
2. Raising the Kenyan flag belongs to Madaraka Day.
3. Bel leaves are offered at Maha Shivratri.

Answer: Paryushan; Madaraka Day; Maha Shivratri.

## Activity: Safety talk and a composition
You will need: Exercise book
1. In groups, list safety rules for a night vigil, a crowded temple or hall, and a national ceremony.
2. Add one inclusion rule and one charity idea.
3. Teach the rules to a partner, especially a partner who needs them repeated slowly and clearly.
4. Write a short composition on one festival, its meaning, two rites and how you will stay safe.

## Practice
1. Match bel leaves, Micchami Dukkadam and the National Anthem to their festivals.
2. Name two safety rules for a festival crowd.
3. Why should a celebration include learners with special needs?

## Summary
• Each festival keeps its own rites.
• Crowds, fire and strangers need clear safety rules.
• Inclusion and charity make the celebration fit the values of unity and patriotism.

### Answers to practice
1. Bel leaves: Maha Shivratri. Micchami Dukkadam: Paryushan. National Anthem: Madaraka Day.
2. Any two: stay with a known adult, do not push, do not play with fire, do not go with a stranger, agree a meeting place.
3. Festivals are for social cohesion and unity. Leaving people out contradicts that meaning.

questions.question: The three festivals in this sub-strand are
options: Maha Shivratri, Paryushan Parva and Madaraka Day
questions.explanation: The design selects these three: one Hindu, one Jain and one national.

questions.question: Maha Shivratri remembers especially
options: The great night of Lord Shiva
The compilation of the Guru Granth Sahib
questions.explanation: It is the Hindu festival of Lord Shiva's great night.

questions.question: Why is Shiva called Neelkanth?
options: Because the poison he drank to protect the world turned his throat blue
Because he wrote the National Anthem
questions.explanation: The churning-of-the-ocean account explains the blue throat.

questions.question: Which set lists rites of Maha Shivratri?
options: Abhishek, bel leaves, Om Namah Shivaya and a vigil
questions.explanation: Those are acts of Shiva worship on that night.

questions.question: Paryushan Parva is
options: A Jain festival of reflection and forgiveness
questions.explanation: Jains observe Paryushan with self-review, ahimsa and forgiveness.

questions.question: Micchami Dukkadam is said in order to
questions.explanation: It is the Jain forgiveness greeting.

questions.question: Madaraka Day is marked on
questions.explanation: 1 June remembers Kenya's internal self-government. Jamhuri Day is 12 December.

questions.question: During the National Anthem a learner should
options: Use the flag as a cape
questions.explanation: Respect for the anthem is part of patriotism on a national day.

questions.question: White on the Kenyan flag stands for
questions.explanation: White stands for peace. Black, red and green stand for the people, the blood shed for freedom, and the land.

questions.question: Which safety rule fits every festival crowd?
questions.answer: Stay with a known adult, do not push, and do not play with fire or go with a stranger.
questions.explanation: Celebration includes care for one another.
